q: The rule of double Jeopardy enunciated in Article 20(2) is based on the principle of
explanation: Art. 20(2) needs both prosecution and punishment, so it embodies autrefois convict (previously convicted), not autrefois acquit (Maqbool Hussain, 1953).

notes.text: - **Double jeopardy:** maxim *nemo debet bis vexari*; Art. 20(2) rests on **autrefois convict** (previously convicted) – both prosecution **and** punishment are needed, so *autrefois acquit* is not covered. CrPC Sec. 300 → **Sec. 337 BNSS**.

q: Article 20(3) is against
explanation: Article 20(3) is against testimonial compulsion – an accused cannot be compelled to be a witness against himself.

explanation: Compelling an accused to be a witness against himself is self-incrimination, barred by Art. 20(3); double jeopardy is 20(2) and ex post facto law 20(1).

q: According to which Article of the Indian Constitution, 'No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once'?
explanation: Article 20(2) provides that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once (double jeopardy).

q: The constitution of India provides certain protections to citizens. In this regard, all statements below are correct, except
options: No person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once
Parliament of India shall be competent to make a criminal law with retrospective effect
No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself
Safeguards provided in Article 22 are not available to a person arrested or detained under preventive Detention law
key_text: Parliament of India shall be competent to make a criminal law with retrospective effect
explanation: Art. 20(1) bars conviction or a heavier penalty under an ex post facto law, so Parliament cannot make a criminal law with retrospective effect. The other three statements (20(2), 20(3), 22(3) exclusion of preventive detainees) are correct.

notes.text: - **Ex post facto law** = a **retrospective** law (not prospective, not a Bill). Hence **Parliament cannot** make a **criminal law with retrospective effect** that convicts or enhances punishment.

q: No one ought to be punished twice for the same offence is based on the
explanation: 'No one shall be punished twice for the same offence' is the doctrine of double jeopardy (Art. 20(2)); eclipse and repugnancy are unrelated doctrines.

notes.text: - **Double jeopardy:** maxim *nemo debet bis vexari*; Art. 20(2) rests on **autrefois convict** (previously convicted) – both prosecution **and** punishment are needed, so *autrefois acquit* is not covered. CrPC Sec. 300 → **Sec. 337 BNSS**.

q: Every Ex Post Facto Law
explanation: An ex post facto law is a retrospective law; Art. 20(1) forbids such laws in criminal matters.

notes.text: - **Ex post facto law** = a **retrospective** law (not prospective, not a Bill). Hence **Parliament cannot** make a **criminal law with retrospective effect** that convicts or enhances punishment.

q: Which Article of Indian constitution prohibits employment of children in factories?
explanation: Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories.

q: In which year was the bill related to abolishing bonded labour passed?
explanation: The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act was passed in 1976 (it replaced the ordinance of 1975), giving effect to Article 23.

notes.text: - **Explanation II:** "**Hindus**" includes **Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists** – **not Parsis**.

q: The Sikhs in India are permitted to carry Kirpan. Under which one of the Fundamental Rights are they permitted to do so?
explanation: Explanation I to Art. 25 makes wearing and carrying the kirpan part of the profession of Sikhism – so it is the Right to Freedom of Religion. (No key was printed.)

q: The Constitution of India grants religious freedom to the citizens. In this regard, all statements below are correct except
options: Right to religion is available to Indian citizens without any limitations
The State will not compel any citizen to pay any taxes for the promotion of any particular religion
Religious instructions are totally banned in State owned educational institutions
In Non-State owned educational institutions religious instruction is not totally prohibited but it must not be imposed upon people of other religions without their consent
key_text: Right to religion is available to Indian citizens without any limitations
explanation: Religious freedom is not unlimited: Art. 25 is subject to public order, morality, health and other Part III provisions. Art. 27 (no tax for one religion) and Art. 28(1)/(3) (no instruction in wholly State-funded institutions; voluntary elsewhere) are correct.

notes.text: - **Begar** = involuntary forced labour **without payment**, exacted by officials/zamindars.

q: Which article of the Constitution prescribes that Hindu religious institutions of public character shall be open to all classes and sections of Hindus?
explanation: Article 25(2)(b) – throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes of Hindus.

notes.text: - **Arts. 21A and 24** together (education + no hazardous work) make the right meaningful for children (**APPSC G1 2023**).

q: "...all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practice and propagate religion" is mentioned in which Article?
explanation: The quoted words are from Article 25(1).

notes.text: - **23(1):** prohibits **traffic in human beings, begar** and other **forced labour**; available to **citizens and non-citizens**, and protects against the **State and private persons**.

q: Right of religion in India is ?
explanation: Freedom of religion (Arts. 25-28) is a Fundamental Right.

notes.text: - **23(2):** State may impose **compulsory service for public purposes** (military/social service); it need not pay in every case, but may **not discriminate on religion, race, caste or class**.

q: A sale of immovable property of an endowment institution is void as per Section 81 of the Endowments Act if
options: it has taken place prior to the commencement of Act 30/1987, with the permission of the Government
it has taken place prior to the commencement of Act 30/1987, with the permission of the Commissioner
it has taken place without the permission of the Government or Commissioner, either prior to or after the commencement of Act 30/1987
key_text: it has taken place without the permission of the Government or Commissioner, either prior to or after the commencement of Act 30/1987
explanation: Under Section 81 of the AP Endowments Act 30 of 1987, a sale of endowment immovable property made without the sanction of the Government/Commissioner – before or after the Act – is void.

notes.text: - Indian pluralism also protects language: **Art. 343** – **Hindi** (Devanagari) is the **official language of the Union**; India has **no national language**.

q: Which authority has to initiate action in case of group encroachment on Endowments lands?
explanation: Key as printed: under the AP Endowments Act 1987 the Deputy Commissioner initiates action against group encroachment of endowment lands.

q: Who is the competent authority to sanction budget to the temples published under 6-C category?
explanation: Key as printed: the Assistant Commissioner sanctions the budgets of 6(c) institutions (lowest-income temples) under the AP Endowments Act.

notes.text: - **Sarva Dharma Sambhava** = state neutrality + **positive intervention for reform**.

q: Who is competent to file petition for eviction of an encroacher before the Endowments Tribunal?
explanation: Key as printed: the Assistant Commissioner files the eviction petition before the Endowments Tribunal against encroachers.

q: Who has to represent the institution/ temple in the legal proceedings before the Court of Law?
explanation: Under the AP Endowments Act the Executive Officer manages the temple and represents the institution in legal proceedings.

notes.text: - **Articles 25–28** emphasise the secular character of Part III; also Arts. 14–16, 29–30, **325** (no exclusion from rolls on religion).

q: Who is competent to grant permission for sale of land of a temple by way of public auction?
explanation: Printed key kept: under the AP Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987, sale of temple land by public auction needs the Commissioner of Endowments' sanction; not verified in the library.
